issues.legal_issue: A temporary injunction in a property dispute must be assessed by considering the claimant’s prima facie case, the balance of convenience, the possibility of irreparable injury, and the parties’ conduct.
material_facts: The claimants sought a temporary injunction in a partition suit, alleging that the disputed properties were joint family properties.
The respondents produced numerous documents indicating that they and their predecessors had dealt with and possessed the properties exclusively for a long time.
The claimants had not exercised acts of possession and had remained inactive while the respondents dealt with the properties.
Construction had begun on the properties, and a respondent was said to have made a substantial investment in development.
The trial court had focused on irreparable injury without adequately considering the other relevant factors.
issues.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to the temporary injunction they sought; the appeals against the order permitting construction were dismissed subject to protective directions.
issues.legal_principle: Temporary injunction is equitable relief. The court must assess whether a prima facie case requiring protection exists, weigh the parties’ respective need for protection, consider the possibility of irreparable injury, and take account of the claimant’s conduct, including whether the claimant approached the court with clean hands. A finding of a prima facie case must also account for the other requirements for an injunction. The Court relied on M. Gurudas v. Rasaranjan, Seema Arshad Zaheer v. Municipal Corpn. of Greater Mumbai, and Transmission Corpn. of A.P. Ltd. v. Lanco Kondapalli Power (P) Ltd.; it also referred to Colgate Palmolive and S.M. Dyechem in discussing American Cyanamid, but did not decide that debate.

rule.if: temporary_injunction_application and property_partition_dispute and claimant_long_inactive and defendants_exclusive_dealing and claimant_no_acts_of_possession and construction_underway

predicates.temporary_injunction_application: The claimant applied for an interim order restraining dealings with or construction on disputed property.
predicates.property_partition_dispute: The proceeding sought partition of property claimed to be jointly held.
predicates.claimant_long_inactive: The claimant waited for a long time while the opposing side dealt with the property.
predicates.defendants_exclusive_dealing: The opposing side and its predecessors dealt with or possessed the property exclusively for a long time.
predicates.claimant_no_acts_of_possession: The claimant did not exercise acts of possession over the property.
predicates.construction_underway: Construction on the disputed property had begun when interim relief was considered.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks interim protection in a property partition dispute after remaining inactive while the opposing side dealt with the property exclusively, with no acts of possession by the claimant and construction underway, the rule describes the denial of the temporary injunction.

issues.legal_issue: Construction already underway may be allowed to continue during a property suit where stopping it would be improper, provided the construction and any resulting interests remain subject to the suit and are protected by safeguards.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned an appeal from interim orders in a partition suit.
Construction had already come up on the disputed property, and a respondent was said to have spent a substantial sum on development.
The Court considered that the construction should not be stopped at that stage, while also requiring that the suit’s final outcome govern the construction and any third-party interests.

The Court directed that documents creating third-party interests disclose that the matter was sub judice and that the interests were subject to the suit, and required the respondents to furnish security.
issues.conclusion: The appeals were dismissed subject to permission for construction to continue, the construction and any third-party interests being subject to the final decision in the suit, and the respondents furnishing security.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding interim relief, courts must consider the consequences of granting or refusing an injunction and endeavour to protect all parties’ interests. The valuable nature of property alone does not justify an injunction. Where construction has already come up and substantial development expenditure has been made, the court may allow construction to continue while making it subject to the suit and requiring safeguards for the claimant’s interest. The Court relied on the equitable principles governing injunctions discussed in M. Gurudas v. Rasaranjan, Seema Arshad Zaheer v. Municipal Corpn. of Greater Mumbai, and Transmission Corpn. of A.P. Ltd. v. Lanco Kondapalli Power (P) Ltd. No statutory provision was identified for this ruling.

rule.if: interlocutory_injunction_appeal_in_partition_suit and construction_already_underway and substantial_development_investment and third_party_interests_can_be_disclosed and security_can_be_furnished

predicates.interlocutory_injunction_appeal_in_parti: A party appealed an interim injunction decision in a suit seeking partition of disputed property.
predicates.construction_already_underway: Construction on the disputed property had already begun or had substantially come up.
predicates.substantial_development_investment: A party had made a substantial investment in developing the property.
predicates.third_party_interests_can_be_disclosed: Documents creating interests for others could state that those interests were subject to the pending suit.
predicates.security_can_be_furnished: The party continuing construction could furnish security to protect the opposing party’s interest.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns interim relief in a partition suit, construction is already underway, substantial development investment has been made, and third-party interests and the opposing party’s interest can be protected, the rule describes allowing construction to continue subject to the suit’s outcome and security.
